newsitem.title: CANADA: ATHLETICS-JOHNSON AND BAILEY RACE FOR MONEY AND PRESTIGE.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-JOHNSON AND BAILEY RACE FOR MONEY AND PRESTIGE.

text.p: The world's two greatest sprinters line up on Sunday for big bucks and the right to the title of world's fastest human over a distance which will be a mystery to both.

World 100 metres record holder and Olympic champion Donovan Bailey of Canada takes on 200 metres world record holder and double Olympic gold medalist Michael Johnson in a 150 metres at an extravaganza entitled: "One to One Challenge of Champions."

A head-to-head showdown of champions at the SkyDome is the central theme to this entertainment spectacle, a made-for-television showcase that is being kicked off with a tickertape parade on Friday through downtown Toronto.
Since the main event will last only about 15 seconds, a number of other head-to-head showdowns will be featured.
A long jump duel will pit American Jackie Joyner-Kersee against her long time rival Heike Dreschler of Germany.

Olympic women's 100 metres champion Gail Devers of the United States will take on Olympic 100 metres hurdles champion Ludmila Engquist of Sweden in the high hurdles. Devers won the 1993 world title over the hurdles.
Pole vault world record holder Sergei Bubka of Ukraine has pulled out of his showdown with South African Okkert Brits and been replaced by American Lawrence Johnson.
These events plus a Blues Brothers concert will provide the backdrop for the Bailey-Johnson duel.

Bailey, who posted a record 9.84 seconds in winning Atlanta 100 meters gold, and Johnson, who clocked 19.32 to win the 200, will each earn $500,000 just for showing up. The winner will pocket another $1 million.

Both claim to be the word's fastest human and both insist they expect to win. But the race is a handicapper's delight, or nightmare, since there is no track record for either sprinter over this distance.

None other than sprinter Ben Johnson, whose 1988 Olympic steroid scandal brought disgrace to Canadian athletics, has picked American Johnson over Bailey, the man who restored Canada's honour on the track.
"I think Johnson has the edge, but it will be very close," Ben Johnson said, predicting a time of 14.83 seconds.
The special track will start with a 75 metres bend and finish with 75 metres of straightaway.
Johnson will have a clear advantage on the curve, with Bailey possibly having an edge on the straight.
A pair of Canadian academics -- one at a university in Toronto and another in Alberta -- recently dissected Bailey's and Johnson's races at the Atlanta Games and predicted Bailey would win on Sunday.
One leading Canadian athletics official, however, sees it differently. Cecil Smith, a member of the International Amateur Athletic Federation technical committee, predicts Johnson will beat Bailey.

And Smith, a former meeting director and executive director of the Ontario Track and Field Association, has a knack for predictions. In April of last year he forecast that Bailey would win the Olympic 100 metres in world record time. He was right on both counts.
"I think it's interesting stuff," Smith said of the professors' conclusions.
"But I think Johnson will win. It's one thing to train over longer distances like Johnson. But it's another thing running a 150 metres distance which you never race, which is the case with Bailey."

Smith said he believes Bailey is a faster accelerator from about the 30 metres mark to the 100 metres finish line, but is not a fast starter. So Smith expects Bailey to be behind at the midway point, especially since Johnson has far more experience running a curve.
"The question is will Bailey have sufficient time in the straight to bring back Johnson, who I think will have the lead by then," Smith said.
"Bailey will have to put on the squeeze and suddenly he's going to be in oxygen debt after 90 metres because you don't breathe in a 100 metres race. In a 150 metres race you have to breathe.
"Johnson has the ability to pace himself. Can Bailey? We'll see."
